body.heading: Ten minutes, one room, loud music
paragraphs: Tidying feels different with a soundtrack and a deadline. Pick one room, put on three favourite songs, and everyone moves until the music stops. Toys to the basket, cups to the kitchen, cushions back on the sofa, shoes to the door.

Give small children one category at a time — only soft toys, only books — so the job has an edge they can see. Older children can race the clock on a surface: clear the whole table before the song ends.

body.heading: Why it works
paragraphs: The music does two jobs. It sets the pace, and it makes the end obvious, so nobody has to nag. When the last song finishes, the room is visibly better and everyone stops at the same moment, which feels fair.

It also turns a chore into the last event of the day rather than a punishment inside it. Families who disco clean-up after dinner often find children asking for it, which no one has ever said about a silent tidy.

body.heading: Keep it light
paragraphs: Skip inspections. The goal is a room that feels good to sit in, not a room that passes a test. If a corner is still messy when the music ends, it can wait for tomorrow's songs.
Younger children may mostly dance, and that counts as helping. The habit is the thing being built; the spotless room is a bonus that arrives in its own time.

description: Three songs, one room, everybody moving: turning the evening tidy-up into a short, loud, shared game.
